locations.quote: Supervisors should be able to provide their own scientific writing guidelines as well as conventions on the style of theses and proposals. Based on these guidelines, the LLM can provide formative feedback that is restricted to the aspects they cover. Ethically, it is difficult to let LLMs grade a final thesis, as this constitutes normative feedback and requires close scrutiny. Formative feedback, on the other hand, is less critical since it serves as input for students to improve their work.

If a regression occurs or an issue persists across iterations, the previous feedback was likely hard for the student to understand and act on. A regression means an aspect that was previously fine has worsened, while a persistent issue means earlier feedback flagged the same problem and the student has not yet resolved it.

In such cases, the feedback tool should adapt its style, for example by being more explanatory, more verbose, or providing concrete examples that illustrate the desired outcome. Where the feedback tool repeatedly fails to communicate an issue, it should defer the discussion to the supervisor.

locations.quote: Integrating large language models (LLMs) to assist supervisors with non-content-related feedback could improve the thesis writing process. As Figure 1 illustrates, an LLM-powered Reviewer works alongside the supervisor, evaluating the thesis against the research group’s writing guidelines and generating automatic formative feedback [NM06]. This Reviewer covers exactly the repetitive, non-content-related layer of feedback that currently drains supervisors, freeing them to focus on specific content and on discussions with their students, which is key in mentoring environments [BBE10, NM06]. The quality of feedback improves as supervisors have more time to engage deeply with the thesis, leading to better outcomes overall. Additionally, supervisors can provide feedback faster, making the process more scalable.

Supervisors should be able to provide their own scientific writing guidelines as well as conventions on the style of theses and proposals. Based on these guidelines, the LLM can provide formative feedback that is restricted to the aspects they cover. Since guidelines may not already be in a suitable format, the LLM may first need to preprocess them into a structured representation it can act on. **Ethically, it is difficult to let LLMs grade a final thesis, as this constitutes normative feedback and requires close scrutiny.** Formative feedback, on the other hand, is less critical since it serves as input for students to improve their work.

Ethically, it is difficult to let LLMs grade a final thesis, as this constitutes normative feedback and requires close scrutiny. Formative feedback, on the other hand, is less critical since it serves as input for students to improve their work. The idea is that students interpret the feedback themselves and discuss it, either independently or with their supervisor. Therefore, it is less important that every output of the LLM is perfectly correct.

This approach supports several modes of feedback generation. In one mode, no LLM-generated feedback is produced at all and all feedback comes from the supervisor. Alternatively, the student can obtain instant feedback on their proposal or thesis directly from the LLM, while keeping in mind that the supervisor has not reviewed this output. A third mode combines both sources, as illustrated in Figure 2. In this combined mode, multiple specialized agents analyze specific parts of the thesis in parallel. The supervisor then aggregates and reviews the resulting feedback and adds their own feedback. Finally, the supervisor merges both sets and publishes them to the student.

If a regression occurs or an issue persists across iterations, the previous feedback was likely hard for the student to understand and act on. A regression means an aspect that was previously fine has worsened, while a persistent issue means earlier feedback flagged the same problem and the student has not yet resolved it. In such cases, the feedback tool should adapt its style, for example by being more explanatory, more verbose, or providing concrete examples that illustrate
the desired outcome. Where the feedback tool repeatedly fails to communicate an issue, it should defer the discussion to the supervisor.

summary: The proposal has a clear technical direction and a relevant workflow, but it requires substantial revision before it meets the group's guidelines. summary: The proposal is well-structured with a clear problem statement, well-defined objectives, and a realistic iteration-based schedule, and no structural, figure, or schedule issues were identified. The primary weakness is the pervasive use of first-person 'I' (approximately 24 instances), which directly violates the stated style guidelines and requires a systematic rewrite. summary: The proposal addresses a well-defined and technically interesting problem (automating time-limited access provisioning) with a clear four-objective structure and a reasonable schedule. However, it fails to meet several fundamental formatting and structural requirements: the mandatory Abstract is entirely missing, the Problem section violates the no-solution rule, the Introduction lacks an opening paragraph, and the schedule includes a thesis-writing iteration. Widespread use of first-person 'I' (15+ instances), a contraction, a double-verb objective, a generic figure caption, an improperly classified bibliography entry, and the missing AI attestation sentence collectively bring the document well below submission-ready quality. Addressing the critical and major items above is necessary before resubmission.

findings.description: The guidelines state: Avoid 'one,' 'I,' and 'our.' The student uses "I" as the subject in 15+ sentences throughout the Objective, Schedule, and AI Transparency sections. locations.quote: I will build a platform on which any member of the chair requests time-limited access to any resource, a maintainer decides, and the access ends on its own.

I follow the object-oriented software engineering method of Bruegge and Dutoit, and Figure 1 shows the actors and use cases of the platform as a use case diagram in the Unified Modeling Language. I pursue four objectives:
I will replace the flat list of hosts and channels with a resource tree whose inner nodes are folders and whose leaves each carry a binding to one target system.
I will store the tree with a transitive-closure table of ancestor–descendant pairs and cap the fan-out, so that an approval on the root never reaches the whole infrastructure by accident.

I will define one connector contract that validates a binding, grants and revokes access, and optionally lists the current members, and I will implement the keycloak-group, slack-channel, github-team, and webhook connectors on it.
I will build declarative request forms whose fields, visibility conditions, and rules turn answers into requests for a resource path, a level, and a duration.

I will therefore split the approval: in the review step, the resource owner records a decision without changing Keycloak, and in the grant step, the super admin sets membership and expiry atomically, in bulk for a vetted queue.
I will compare the manual administrative actions and the time to working access with the current process.
I will attach a recertification interval to each resource, which its descendants inherit, and open a campaign whenever the interval elapses.
The thesis runs from 1 October 2026 to 31 March 2027, and I divide it into iterations of two to four weeks.
Outcome: the correctness scenarios pass, and I measure the effort.

summary: The proposal addresses a relevant and well-motivated research topic (integrating Artemis with GitLab CI) and contains coherent content in its Problem Statement, Related Work, and Proposed Solution sections. However, it has fundamental structural deficiencies: three required sections (Introduction, Motivation, Objective) are entirely missing, the AI Transparency Statement is absent, the sole figure is a prohibited sequence diagram, the bibliography falls short of the minimum, and the schedule violates multiple agile-structuring rules (no 2-4 week iterations, forbidden writing/documentation items, horizontal layering). Substantial restructuring and rewriting are needed before this proposal can be submitted.

summary: The proposal is well-structured with a clear problem statement, well-defined objectives, a concrete schedule, and appropriate figures; structure, problem/motivation, figures, and schedule sections all passed review without issues. The primary weakness is the pervasive use of first-person singular "I" (~20 instances), which directly violates the stated writing-style guideline and should be replaced with the platform or other actors as subject. Secondary issues include a terminology inconsistency ("compute hosts" vs. "Linux hosts"), a minor gap in the AI transparency statement wording, and a bibliographic formatting suggestion; all are straightforward to fix.

findings.title: Excessive use of first-person singular "I" throughout the main body
findings.description: The writing style guidelines explicitly state to avoid "I." The main body of the proposal (Abstract through Schedule, pages 2–9) uses "I" approximately 20 times (e.g., "I develop," "I evaluate," "I model," "I implement," "I reach this objective," "I divide," "I reserve," and six "I deliver" in the Schedule). The guideline advises using "we" sparingly only for the thesis approach, or restructuring sentences so the platform/actor is the subject. The student should replace most instances of "I" with the platform as subject (e.g., "The platform models resources as a tree…") or use passive-free active constructions. The AI Transparency section (page 12) is a personal disclosure where "I" is expected and can be retained.

locations.quote: In this thesis, **I develop** a self-service platform on which every grant carries an expiry date from the moment somebody requests it.
**I evaluate** the platform at the chair on correctness, administrative effort, and extensibility.
Following the object-oriented software engineering method of Bruegge and Dutoit, **I pursue** four objectives:
**I model** the resources as a tree whose folders pass maintainership, audit policy, and grants down to leaves bound to target systems.
**I implement** the keycloak-group, slack-channel, github-team, and webhook connectors, whose credentials administrators configure at runtime.
**I reach** this objective when the webhook connector, written after **I freeze** the framework, needs one new class and one registry entry.
**I evaluate** correctness with an automated scenario that provisions SSH, Slack, and GitHub access from one approval.
**I reach** this objective when each access disappears after expiry and, in a second run with the workflow engine disabled on purpose, the drift check reports the remaining SSH membership.
Keycloak gates its workflow API on a realm-wide administrative role that maintainers must not hold, so **I split** each decision into a review step.
**I reach** this objective when administrators perform fewer manual actions and requesters wait less than in the current process.
**I reach** this objective when the platform answers, for any grant, who requested it and why, who reviewed and granted it, when it ended, and who confirmed it since.
**I divide** the work into six iterations of four weeks, each ending with a vertically integrated increment that a user can try in the web application.
**I reserve** the final two weeks, from 18 to 31 March 2027, as buffer for features that slip from earlier iterations.
Iteration 1, 1–28 October (Objective 1): **I deliver** the Keycloak realm with OpenID Connect login, SSH key self-service, and the resource tree with inherited maintainers.

findings.title: AI transparency statement omits the explicit purpose clause (correctness and coherence)
findings.description: The transparency statement says 'I carefully checked all AI-generated text, revised it where necessary, verified every citation against the original publication, and compiled and inspected every diagram.' While this confirms the author checked the text, the guidelines call for language similar to 'I have carefully checked all texts created with these tools to ensure that they are correct and make sense.' summary: The proposal addresses a well-motivated and technically interesting problem with a clearly structured set of four objectives, a concrete architecture, and a realistic iteration-based schedule. However, three critical violations (missing Abstract, a solution embedded in the Problem section, and a schedule entry for thesis writing) combined with numerous major issues (systematic use of first-person 'I', a documentation source in the bibliography, an undersized figure caption, a single-paragraph objective, missing section introduction, and an incomplete AI transparency statement) mean the document is not yet submission-ready. summary: The proposal addresses a relevant topic (integrating GitLab CI with Artemis for dynamic build plan management) and demonstrates domain knowledge, but it fails to meet most structural requirements: four mandatory sections (Introduction, Motivation, Objectives, AI Transparency Statement) are entirely missing. The schedule is structured as a waterfall with no iteration cadence, the bibliography falls below the minimum, and the single figure is a prohibited sequence diagram. Widespread writing issues (passive voice, forbidden sentence starters, filler words, undefined abbreviations) compound the structural deficiencies, making substantial revision necessary before submission.

findings.title: Missing Introduction section
findings.description: The proposal does not contain an Introduction section. The document proceeds directly from the Abstract to Section 1 'Problem Statement'. An Introduction section is required by the guidelines and must be less than one page in length.

findings.title: Missing dedicated Motivation section
findings.description: The proposal contains no standalone Motivation section in the body text. The guidelines require a Motivation section (at most 3/4 page) that is visionary, explaining why it is scientifically important to solve the problem and focusing on the positive aspects of having the solution. The Abstract includes a brief 'Motivation/Objective' sentence and Section 5 'Expected Findings' touches on long-term benefits, but neither constitutes a proper Motivation section. Without this section, the visionary framing and the requirement to avoid repeating the Problem cannot be demonstrated.

findings.title: Missing Objectives section with subsections in action form
findings.description: The proposal has no 'Objectives' section structured as required. Section 4 is 'System Requirements and Top Level Design' and Section 5 is 'Expected Findings', neither of which fulfills the requirement. The required structure is: a short introductory paragraph, a bullet list of 3-4 high-level objectives in action form (each fitting in one line, no double verbs), followed by a dedicated subsection for each objective (at least two paragraphs per subsection with detailed descriptions). Section 5 is written in expectation form ('We expect to use…') rather than action form and contains no subsections.

findings.title: AI Transparency Statement is entirely missing
findings.description: The proposal does not contain an AI Transparency Statement section, which is listed as a required section. The statement must: (1) be written in first person, (2) name specific AI tools used and their purposes, (3) specify which sections of the proposal the tools were used for, and (4) include a confirmation sentence such as 'I have carefully checked all texts created with these tools to ensure that they are correct and make sense.' The student must add a dedicated 'AI Transparency Statement' section (typically after the Schedule and before/after References) addressing all of these points.

summary: The proposal addresses a relevant and well-scoped topic (integrating Artemis with GitLab CI), but it is severely deficient in structure and completeness: three required sections (Introduction, Motivation, Objectives) are entirely missing, the AI Transparency Statement is absent, only one figure and five references are provided, and the schedule is not organized into agile iterations and includes non-permissible thesis-writing tasks. The writing quality is passable but contains multiple short paragraphs, vague language, and minor formatting inconsistencies. Substantial rework is needed before this proposal can be considered submission-ready.

findings.title: Missing Introduction section
findings.description: The proposal does not contain a dedicated Introduction section. After the Abstract, the document jumps directly to '1 Problem Statement'. An Introduction section is required by the guidelines and must be less than one page.

findings.title: Missing Motivation section
findings.description: The proposal lacks a dedicated Motivation section as required by the guidelines (at most 3/4 page). The closest content is a single sentence in the Abstract ('Motivation/Objective: Since some Version Control (VC) systems include a Continuous Integration (CI) application...') and parts of Section 5 'Expected Findings.' Neither constitutes a proper visionary Motivation section that explains why the problem is scientifically important to solve and focuses on the positive aspects of having the solution. A standalone Motivation section must be added.

locations.quote: Motivation/Objective: Since some Version Control (VC) systems include a Continuous Integration (CI) application, it is possible to reduce the efort required to maintain the servers and migrate the CI service from external applications as Jenkins to the inbuilt CI service.

On long term, we expect that more universities will use Artemis, since the setup hurdle will become smaller. As described in section 3, this might lead to better developers and better code, due to the fact, that more students will be taught the concepts of CI.

findings.title: Missing Objectives section with required subsection structure
findings.description: The proposal has no 'Objectives' section with subsections as required by the guidelines. Section 4 is titled 'System Requirements and Top Level Design' and Section 5 is 'Expected Findings,' but neither constitutes a proper Objectives section. The guidelines require a short introduction, a bullet list of 3-4 high-level objectives (each fitting in one line, in action form), followed by a dedicated subsection for each objective of at least two paragraphs. None of this structure is present. The student must add a dedicated section titled 'Objectives' with at least two subsections, each beginning with a single action verb and containing at least two paragraphs of detailed description.

summary: The proposal has a solid foundation: structure, problem statement, objectives, bibliography, and figures all pass review. However, there are six major issues that need addressing before submission—primarily mechanical writing violations (forbidden sentence starters, overlong paragraphs mixing distinct ideas) in the Motivation and Objective sections, plus two schedule problems (a documentation item and a waterfall-style final iteration with an unmeasurable deliverable). These are all fixable with targeted edits, but the accumulation of paragraph-splitting and sentence-restructuring work in the core narrative sections means the proposal is not yet ready to submit as-is.

findings.title: Motivation second paragraph exceeds 10 lines and mixes distinct ideas
findings.description: The second paragraph of the Motivation section spans approximately 12 rendered lines (continuing from page 4 to page 5). It combines three distinct ideas: (1) students benefit from faster feedback, (2) a detailed explanation of self-regulated learning theory (knowledge, beliefs, interpretation of guidelines), and (3) the practical advantage of instant LLM-powered feedback. Split the paragraph after the first sentence or after the self-regulated-learning explanation to keep each paragraph focused on one idea and within the 5-8 line range.

locations.quote: Better and faster feedback has signifcant advantages for students as well. When feedback arrives sooner, students can act on it while the writing process is still fresh in their minds. The student brings both knowledge, comprising theoretical and practical domain expertise, and beliefs about how to approach the task and how to work and write scientifcally, which include the student's personal interpretation of the writing guidelines. Drawing on this knowledge and these beliefs, the student writes the thesis. Through self-regulated learning, the student engages with the Reviewer's feedback, refecting on it independently or

discussing it with the supervisor, and uses it to improve their knowledge, beliefs, and broader strategy for proceeding with the work [NM06]. Because the feedback tool is powered by LLMs, students can obtain instant formative feedback at any point during the writing process.

summary: The proposal passed all review checks across structure, problem/motivation/objectives, bibliography, figures, writing style, formatting, AI transparency, and schedule with no actionable issues identified. The document appears well-organized, clearly written, and complete in all required sections. It is ready for submission in its current form.

The proposal presents a well-motivated and technically detailed project on automated resource access management, with clear objectives and a reasonable architecture. However, it has a critical structural gap (the mandatory Abstract is entirely missing) and seven major issues spanning logic (problem section leaking a solution), structural length violations, inconsistent terminology, a prohibited double-verb formulation, an under-described figure caption, a contraction, and an incomplete AI transparency statement. Addressing these issues—particularly adding the Abstract, trimming and refocusing the Problem section, and unifying terminology—will bring the proposal up to submission-ready quality.

summary: The proposal addresses a relevant and interesting topic (connecting Artemis with GitLab CI) and shows a reasonable understanding of the problem, but it fails to meet several mandatory structural requirements: the Introduction, Motivation, and Objectives sections are entirely absent, the AI Transparency Statement is missing, and the figure requirements (at least two diagrams, no sequence diagrams) are not fulfilled. findings.title: Horizontal layering across Iterations 1–3 instead of vertically integrated features

summary: A strong, well-structured proposal. summary: The topic is well scoped and the problem/related-work writing is mostly sound, but the proposal deviates significantly from the required structure. Six critical gaps: no Introduction, no Motivation section, no Objective section with the required bullet list of 3-4 action-form objectives and two-paragraph subsections, no AI Transparency Statement, only 5 bibliography entries (minimum 6-8), and only one figure (minimum two). The single figure is additionally a forbidden sequence diagram. Other major issues: pervasive passive voice, four sentences starting with forbidden openers (To/Since/In order to), and a schedule built from one-off single-week calendar items rather than 2-4 week agile iterations, which also contains a requirements item and thesis-writing/documentation tasks. Minor issues include undefined "API", filler words, inconsistent "CI server"/"CI service" terminology, a list-style abstract, and several typos. The author should restructure the document around the required section list, rewrite objectives in action form, replace the sequence diagram with a UML activity/component diagram plus one additional figure, and rebuild the schedule as iterations with measurable deliverables.

summary: A strong, well-structured proposal. All required sections are present and within length limits; the Problem section isolates actors (requesters, maintainers, auditors) without proposing solutions; the Motivation is visionary without repeating the Problem; all four objectives and their subsection headings are in single-verb action form with two-paragraph subsections. The Bibliography holds 12 peer-reviewed entries in a consistent alpha citation style with citations placed before full stops, and internet sources (Keycloak, Slack, GitHub docs) are correctly footnoted. Three UML figures (use case, object, component) are all referenced in text with long descriptive captions, and no sequence diagrams are used. The AI Transparency Statement is specific (tool, model, date, level, purposes, sections) and confirms the author checked all AI-generated text. The Schedule is six 4-week vertically integrated iterations with measurable outcomes, a buffer, no requirements sprint, and no thesis-writing tasks. Two issues found: (1) MAJOR — the body text is written systematically in first-person singular "I" (abstract, Section 4, Schedule), against the group rule to avoid "I" and prefer "we"/third person; (2) MINOR — the Bruegge & Dutoit book, a legitimate bibliography source, is cited only via a commercial store-page URL footnote instead of a proper reference entry. Fixing the voice issue and adding the book entry would bring the proposal to a clean state.

summary: The proposal is substantively strong — a concrete, well-observed problem with clearly identified actors, 13 references (12 peer-reviewed), two informative UML diagrams both referenced in the text, and a mostly agile, vertically integrated 7-iteration schedule. findings.title: Schedule contains a thesis-writing/presentation iteration
findings.description: Iteration 7 is dedicated entirely to 'Write the thesis and prepare the final presentation'. The schedule must not include thesis-writing, documentation, or presentation-preparation tasks; it should cover development/research work only. Reallocate the 18-31 March window to development or evaluation work (e.g., final deployment at the chair, the extensibility measurement via the webhook connector, running the correctness scenarios), so the schedule ends with a deliverable increment.
